Iris House - Cape Social Support

By: Liz Fish | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Living with severely disable children is extremely taxing on families. The full time care they require leaves families isolated and under extreme stress and often the disable child bares the brunt. Iris House children's Hospice offers Risk By Care training community workers in specialist care who come and sit with the children for 4-6 hours giving the mother a break to attend to SASSA grants and their own needs. This care model developed in the UK has been pioneered by Sue Van Der Linde in South Africa. The DSD is getting her to train people in Mpumalanga and Northern Province because it is such an effect model. But all this is at risk with the drastic budget cuts facing the country. Vital care that the State simply does not provide

Summary:
Nolo Mbolo is a mother of two autistic children, living in Site C in Khayelitsha. She spent ten years locking her children away until a community worker from Iris House coaxed her to let them in and get help. There 100’s of mothers like Nolo, living with severely disabled children or children with terminal illness who rely on the free services Iris House Children’s Hospice. But what will happen to them at the end of April when R1.5 million is cut off due to the drastic budget cuts for social development?
Sue Van Der Linde started Iris House Children Hospice 11 years ago and has dedicated her life to create a haven and respite for parents with children living life-threatening and life-limiting conditions. She has trained over 35 community-based home carers in palliative care who work in communities across the Western Cape. This free service cares for over 670 children and encompasses not only conventional care but also essential elements such as equine therapy, medical training, food parcels, social worker support/counselling, and palliative care support.
Iris House has a unique care model called “Risk by Care” based on care models in the UK. It recognises that living with a child with chronic illness is enormously taxing for the family, they can’t leave their child to get shopping or other daily tasks done, and families burn out and get isolated.
Iris House’s 35 community workers go to the families’ homes and care for the children for a few hours to give the mother time out, as well as emotional and medical support. It’s done on an ad hoc basis when the families reach out for help. They also have access times a week to the hospice at Iris House to drop their children for the whole day. Severely disable children are fetched.
Sue says this model enables a far greater impact than providing beds and permanent care at the hospice, creating an extensive network of support for these families.
Sue hasn’t always been into palliative care, she only found her calling at 38 leaving behind a successful corporate career as a buyer for Edcon in Johannesburg. After a series of life-threatening experiences, she left the country and at a loss of what to do with herself in the UK she volunteered at a local children’s hospice in Dorset. Finally, she found meaning and joy. Qualifying in palliative care at Bournemouth College she returned to South Africa 13 years ago. She started out running a children’s hospice from her home in Vergelegen.
We will follow Nolo who became a community carer and now manages the 10 community carers in her area. She knows firsthand the stigma and isolation of mothering autistic children. Sue sent her on the Autism Navigator course and she is now the autism spokesperson for Iris House training parents and teachers about the condition.
Sue has faced many funding challenges and often pays the salaries out of her own pocket but loosing 40% of her budget at the end of April will be devastating. National Government's plans to cut R642.2 million in conditional grants and has a shortfall of R1.1 billion in the wages budget.
Sue is fighting hard for their survival to somehow find the additional R1.5 million to keep their services to these destitute families and their children going. She launched a signature campaign “not without a fight” a crown funding campaign “ Give and Gain” and a “Carers at home” service with well-trained carers which will be a paid service.

Erin: So let's talk about …..the survey that the network has done on the potential impact.

VO: They depend on the Department of social Development to provide that funding.
Natalie: NPO’s…….used to be classified as charity, where as NPO’s are not charities. We are doing the work of government. Government is mandated to serve the vulnerable
VO: Western Cape Social Development funds over 1000 NGOs and fear the 10% cut will destroy many of them and the resources built up over decades.
Robert: NGOs are a critical partner and an integral part of our service delivery model. It means a serious risk for the department's services overall and for the vulnerable people that we serve. Erin “.Are you angry.

Robert “We are trying to protect the most crucial services and we're trying to protect organizations from closing.
Erin “Can you imagine what it would have been like if Iris House hadn't been there?
Gillian: Huh I'm getting cold. Shivers I dont know how I would have gotten through, I still fall back onto Iris House
Nolo “ I don't know how they going to cope without Iris House, because I visit the families, I saw what they need, they need Iris house a lot

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Living with severely disable children is extremely taxing on families. The full time care they require leaves families isolated and under extreme stress and often the disable child bares the brunt. Iris House children's Hospice offers Risk By Care training community workers in specialist care who come and sit with the children for 4-6 hours giving the mother a break to attend to SASSA grants and their own needs. This care model developed in the UK has been pioneered by Sue Van Der Linde in South Africa. The DSD is getting her to train people in Mpumalanga and Northern Province because it is such an effect model. But all this is at risk with the drastic budget cuts facing the country. Vital care that the State simply does not provide
metadata.Summary: Nolo Mbolo is a mother of two autistic children, living in Site C in Khayelitsha. She spent ten years locking her children away until a community worker from Iris House coaxed her to let them in and get help. There 100’s of mothers like Nolo, living with severely disabled children or children with terminal illness who rely on the free services Iris House Children’s Hospice. But what will happen to them at the end of April when R1.5 million is cut off due to the drastic budget cuts for social development? Sue Van Der Linde started Iris House Children Hospice 11 years ago and has dedicated her life to create a haven and respite for parents with children living life-threatening and life-limiting conditions. She has trained over 35 community-based home carers in palliative care who work in communities across the Western Cape. This free service cares for over 670 children and encompasses not only conventional care but also essential elements such as equine therapy, medical training, food parcels, social worker support/counselling, and palliative care support. Iris House has a unique care model called “Risk by Care” based on care models in the UK. It recognises that living with a child with chronic illness is enormously taxing for the family, they can’t leave their child to get shopping or other daily tasks done, and families burn out and get isolated. Iris House’s 35 community workers go to the families’ homes and care for the children for a few hours to give the mother time out, as well as emotional and medical support. It’s done on an ad hoc basis when the families reach out for help. They also have access times a week to the hospice at Iris House to drop their children for the whole day. Severely disable children are fetched. Sue says this model enables a far greater impact than providing beds and permanent care at the hospice, creating an extensive network of support for these families. Sue hasn’t always been into palliative care, she only found her calling at 38 leaving behind a successful corporate career as a buyer for Edcon in Johannesburg. After a series of life-threatening experiences, she left the country and at a loss of what to do with herself in the UK she volunteered at a local children’s hospice in Dorset. Finally, she found meaning and joy. Qualifying in palliative care at Bournemouth College she returned to South Africa 13 years ago. She started out running a children’s hospice from her home in Vergelegen. We will follow Nolo who became a community carer and now manages the 10 community carers in her area. She knows firsthand the stigma and isolation of mothering autistic children. Sue sent her on the Autism Navigator course and she is now the autism spokesperson for Iris House training parents and teachers about the condition. Sue has faced many funding challenges and often pays the salaries out of her own pocket but loosing 40% of her budget at the end of April will be devastating. National Government's plans to cut R642.2 million in conditional grants and has a shortfall of R1.1 billion in the wages budget. Sue is fighting hard for their survival to somehow find the additional R1.5 million to keep their services to these destitute families and their children going. She launched a signature campaign “not without a fight” a crown funding campaign “ Give and Gain” and a “Carers at home” service with well-trained carers which will be a paid service.
